bio: Calgary band The New Electric is a Canadian pop and alternative group formed in 2013 whose polished, hook-driven sound earned national radio and emerging-artist attention.

Formed in Vancouver in the late 1990s around A.C. Newman, The New Pornographers brought together musicians whose other projects already stretched across Canada's independent scene, including Neko Case and Dan Bejar. The group's 2000 debut Mass Romantic immediately established its defining language: stacked harmonies, abrupt melodic turns, dense arrangements and power-pop hooks delivered with the scale and intricacy of a much larger rock band.

Electric Version sharpened that approach, while 2005's Twin Cinema became a high point for the collective and earned a place on the inaugural Polaris Music Prize shortlist. Later records such as Challengers opened more space for acoustic texture and slower pacing without abandoning the band's central strength: several distinctive songwriters and voices functioning inside one recognizable ensemble. The shifting membership became a feature rather than a weakness, allowing the catalogue to absorb parallel careers without losing its identity.

The New Pornographers helped make Canadian indie rock internationally legible during the 2000s without smoothing away its eccentricities. Their Vancouver origins, cross-project membership and sustained critical reach made them an important counterpart to the era's Montréal and Toronto scenes, while their catalogue demonstrated how ambitious arrangement and immediate pop songwriting could occupy the same space.
Vancouver band Odds is a Canadian alternative-rock and power-pop group whose melodic songwriting produced a run of national hits and multiple Juno nominations.

The Philosopher Kings formed in the Toronto area in the early 1990s and quickly distinguished themselves through a blend of R&B, soul, jazz, funk and pop that relied as much on musicianship as studio polish. Fronted by Gerald Eaton, the group built its early reputation through live performance before its self-titled debut established songs such as "Charms" and "Lay My Body Down." The record won the 1996 JUNO Award for Best R&B/Soul Recording, giving the band a prominent place in a Canadian R&B scene that still had limited mainstream infrastructure.

Their second studio album, Famous, Rich and Beautiful, broadened the audience with "Hurts to Love You" and a more refined pop-soul sound; the song earned a 1999 JUNO nomination for Best Single, while the album was nominated for Best Pop Album. What made the group unusual was the amount of talent that later radiated outward from its lineup. Eaton built a production and songwriting career as Jarvis Church, while James Bryan McCollum and Jason Levine created Prozzäk, extending the band's influence into a completely different corner of Canadian pop culture.

The Philosopher Kings later returned to recording and touring after a long gap, reinforcing the durability of a catalogue rooted in groove, arrangement and live interplay. Their significance goes beyond a handful of 1990s radio singles: they helped make sophisticated contemporary R&B visible within Canadian pop before the country's urban music ecosystem had achieved its later scale. They also functioned as an incubator for musicians and producers whose work would shape Canadian pop and R&B well beyond the band itself.

The Riveters is a shortened library credit for Rosie and the Riveters, the Saskatoon folk-pop group founded by singer-songwriters Farideh Olsen, Alexis Normand, Allyson Reigh and Melissa Nygren. The Canadian group paired close vocal harmonies with original songs rooted in folk, gospel, soul and feminist themes across albums including Good Clean Fun! and Ms. Behave.
Toronto band The Sarandons makes Canadian indie rock and roots-oriented guitar music shaped by Americana, neo-psychedelia and tightly arranged melodic songwriting.

Formed in Saskatoon in 2004, The Sheepdogs built their audience the slow way, touring and self-releasing records around a sound rooted in 1970s blues-rock, Southern rock and harmony-heavy classic rock. Their national breakthrough arrived in 2011 through Rolling Stone's Choose the Cover competition, which made them the first unsigned band to appear on the magazine's cover. The exposure turned years of independent work into a major-label opportunity and gave a Saskatchewan band playing deliberately unfashionable guitar music an international platform.

The momentum carried into Learn & Burn and the self-titled The Sheepdogs, produced by Patrick Carney of the Black Keys. At the 2012 JUNO Awards, the group won Rock Album of the Year, New Group of the Year and Single of the Year for "I Don't Know," cementing the breakthrough as more than a magazine-contest novelty. Albums including Future Nostalgia and Changing Colours followed as the band refined its mix of twin guitars, organ, vocal harmonies and compact songwriting.

Rather than pivot away from classic-rock language as trends changed, The Sheepdogs turned stylistic consistency into a long-term identity. Their catalogue, extensive touring and multiple JUNO wins have made them one of the most visible rock bands to emerge from Saskatchewan in the 21st century. That regional story matters: their success demonstrated that a band far from Canada's largest music-industry centres could build a national audience through touring, independent persistence and an immediately recognizable sound.
Toronto group The Slakadeliqs is a Canadian soul and R&B project fronted by producer Slakah the Beatchild, blending warm live instrumentation with modern soul songwriting.
Toronto group The Sorority was a Canadian hip-hop collective formed by Keysha Freshh, Lex Leosis, Haviah Mighty and pHoenix Pagliacci after a viral all-women cypher.

The Soulmate Collective is a Saskatoon neo-soul, jazz and funk ensemble formed around bassist-producer vbnd. Built from a rotating group of local Saskatchewan musicians including Katie Tupper, Connor Newton, Jesse McMillan and Ayden Draude, the collective became the live and recording band behind vbnd's 2021 album Scum Funk, which accounts for its six Northern Dial library tracks.
Lindsay, Ontario band The Strumbellas is a Canadian folk-rock and indie-pop group known for communal vocals, melodic hooks and the international breakthrough single Spirits.

Formed in Windsor, Ontario, in 1990, The Tea Party built one of the most distinctive sounds in Canada's alternative-rock era. Jeff Martin, Stuart Chatwood and Jeff Burrows combined heavy rock and progressive structures with acoustic instruments and musical ideas drawn from the Middle East, India and North Africa, a combination that was often described as "Moroccan roll." Splendor Solis established the band's national audience, while 1995's The Edges of Twilight became a major Canadian success through songs such as "The Bazaar," "Sister Awake" and "Fire in the Head."

Transmission pushed the trio toward darker industrial textures before Triptych produced one of their largest radio songs, "Heaven Coming Down." The Tea Party's albums repeatedly balanced mainstream rock weight with arrangements involving instruments and scales rarely heard on Canadian commercial radio. That approach also translated strongly overseas, particularly in Australia, where the band developed a substantial touring following. By the early 2000s, The Interzone Mantras and Seven Circles had extended the catalogue before the trio split in 2005.

The band reunited in 2011 and resumed touring, later releasing The Ocean at the End and new EP material. Their long-term importance lies in making musical curiosity compatible with arena-ready Canadian rock. The Tea Party occupied the same broad 1990s ecosystem as grunge and post-grunge acts but refused a narrow guitar-band template, creating a catalogue whose global instrumentation and progressive ambition still makes it unusually recognizable.
The Tenors is a Canadian operatic-pop vocal group known for blending classical repertoire with contemporary pop, rock and folk in a multi-platinum international career.

Formed by musicians from Antigonish, Nova Scotia before establishing themselves in Ontario, The Trews broke nationally with 2003's House of Ill Fame. “Not Ready to Go” and “Tired of Waiting” turned the band into a fixture of Canadian rock radio, combining the directness of classic guitar rock with a live intensity developed through years of club touring. The debut's success gave the group a durable audience at a time when Canadian mainstream rock was moving between post-grunge, alternative and rootsier sounds.

Den of Thieves and No Time for Later expanded the catalogue with heavier riffs, ballads and increasingly polished songwriting, while Hope & Ruin showed a band comfortable moving beyond the sound of its first radio breakthrough. “Highway of Heroes,” written in response to the repatriation route for fallen Canadian soldiers, became one of the group's most culturally specific songs and added another dimension to a catalogue often defined by performance energy.

The Trews' significance is rooted in longevity rather than one dramatic reinvention. They carried an East Coast identity into a national touring career, accumulated a large body of Canadian rock-radio staples and remained an active live band across changing industry cycles. Two decades after House of Ill Fame, the record's anniversary treatment reflected how thoroughly those early songs had entered the country's rock repertoire.
Winnipeg band The Watchmen is a Canadian alternative-rock group that became one of the country's most successful rock acts of the 1990s with a run of platinum and gold albums.
Vancouver band The Zolas is a Canadian indie-rock group known for melodic, keyboard-rich alternative pop and a catalogue that has earned national radio play and Juno recognition.

Formed in Winnipeg in 1988, The Watchmen built their reputation through relentless touring before releasing McLaren Furnace Room in 1992. Daniel Greaves's resonant vocals and Joey Serlin's guitar writing gave the band an immediately identifiable centre, and songs such as "Run and Hide" helped move them from Prairie clubs into the national Canadian rock circuit. Their second album, In the Trees, became the decisive breakthrough: "Boneyard Tree," "All Uncovered" and "Lusitana" drove the record to platinum certification in Canada and confirmed the group as one of Winnipeg's most visible rock exports of the 1990s.

Brand New Day followed in 1996 and earned a JUNO nomination for Rock Album of the Year, while 1998's Silent Radar renewed the band's commercial momentum with "Stereo," "Any Day Now" and "Say Something." The album also experimented with web and CD-ROM features at a moment when bands were beginning to treat digital media as part of the record itself, earning a MuchMusic award for its use of new technology. Across those records, The Watchmen balanced muscular guitar rock with melodic songwriting and Greaves's unusually commanding voice.

The band announced a farewell in 2003 but later reunited for recurring Canadian performances, and the continuing audience for those shows has kept the catalogue active well beyond its original radio era. The Watchmen's significance is partly regional and partly national: they demonstrated how a Winnipeg band could build a major Canadian career through touring, durable albums and songs that became fixtures of 1990s rock radio without surrendering the identity of where they came from.
Toronto R&B singer-songwriter THEHONESTGUY, born Mubarak Adeyemi, is a Nigerian-Canadian artist whose warm, groove-led soul blends classic R&B, gospel, jazz and Nigerian musical influence.

Theo Day is a Canadian indie-folk and Americana singer-songwriter emerging from Montreal's independent music scene. Since debuting in 2025, his acoustic storytelling and folk-pop sound have powered releases including the Homegrown EP, sold-out Montreal shows and festival appearances including LASSO Montréal.
Toronto's Theo Vandenhoff began as a synth-pop solo project and grew into a four-piece Canadian post-punk band, pairing dark romanticism, driving rhythms and melodic 1980s-informed textures.

Toronto rapper and producer Theology 3, also known as Theo3, is a longtime Canadian hip-hop veteran whose work helped popularize the city's Screwface Capital identity. His catalogue includes The Screwface Capital, Airplane Over One Way Streets and the Morning Bars series, with collaborations spanning Mathematik, DJ Serious, Muneshine, Tanika Charles and other Canadian underground artists.

Formed in North Delta, British Columbia, around the turn of the millennium, Theory of a Deadman became one of the most durable Canadian rock bands to emerge from the post-grunge era. The group was the first act signed to Chad Kroeger's 604 Records, and its 2002 self-titled debut established Tyler Connolly's songwriting voice through a mix of heavy guitars, melodic choruses and blue-collar themes. Subsequent records including Gasoline and Scars & Souvenirs expanded the band's audience, while songs such as "Santa Monica," "Hate My Life" and "Bad Girlfriend" became staples of North American rock radio.

Theory's longevity has depended on changing its palette without abandoning its core. "Bad Girlfriend" became the band's first No. 1 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart, and later singles "Lowlife," "Rx (Medicate)" and "History of Violence" also reached the top of that chart. On Wake Up Call, the band leaned into piano, pop and electronic textures, with "Rx (Medicate)" reframing its sound around the opioid crisis; Say Nothing continued that move toward more topical writing. Dinosaur returned some of the weight of the band's earlier records while keeping the broader production vocabulary developed over the previous decade.

That arc makes Theory of a Deadman more than a holdover from early-2000s post-grunge. The band has maintained a large cross-border audience across multiple rock-radio eras, placing a Delta, B.C. act in the mainstream U.S. rock conversation for more than two decades. Their catalogue connects the Canadian post-grunge boom of the early 2000s with a later generation of radio rock that became more willing to absorb pop, country and electronic ideas.

TheQ. is a French-language hip-hop artist from Quebec's contemporary rap scene. The artist's catalogue includes singles such as 'PRADA' and 'OTR,' released through Self Liberated Records, and appears alongside Quebec City rappers in rap québécois discovery networks. Northern Dial carries TheQ. as part of its current Quebec hip-hop catalogue.

TheRa11n is a Winnipeg-born Plains Cree artist whose music combines hip-hop with Indigenous musical and cultural influences. His work has been described through a powwow-step approach that connects contemporary production with his Plains Cree identity. Northern Dial carries TheRa11n as part of its Indigenous Canadian hip-hop catalogue.
Chilliwack band These Kids Wear Crowns is a Canadian power-pop and pop-rock group that broke nationally through MuchMusic's disBand and the album Jumpstart.
Scarborough-born poet and rapper Joshua 'Scribe' Watkis is a Canadian hip-hop and spoken-word artist, educator and national poetry champion whose work centers storytelling and community engagement.

Three Days Grace grew out of the small-town Ontario band Groundswell, formed by Adam Gontier, Brad Walst and Neil Sanderson in the Norwood area before the musicians regrouped under their current name in the late 1990s. After signing with Jive, the 2003 self-titled debut turned the band's tense, emotionally direct post-grunge into an international rock-radio breakthrough. "I Hate Everything About You" became the signature early hit, while the album established a formula built around heavy guitar hooks, blunt emotional conflict and choruses designed for large rooms rather than underground scenes.

The 2006 album One-X expanded the band's reach with "Animal I Have Become," "Pain" and "Never Too Late," songs that connected especially strongly with listeners drawn to the catalogue's writing about isolation, addiction and survival. Life Starts Now and Transit of Venus extended the Adam Gontier era before he left the group in 2013. Matt Walst, Brad Walst's brother and the singer of My Darkest Days, stepped in as frontman for Human, Outsider and Explosions, allowing Three Days Grace to remain one of North America's most consistent mainstream-rock acts through a major lineup change.

The band entered another unusual chapter when Gontier returned alongside Walst rather than replacing him, creating a dual-frontman lineup for 2025's Alienation. The reunion produced a new run of No. 1 rock-radio singles, including "Mayday" and "Kill Me Fast." By 2026, Three Days Grace had scored 20 No. 1s on Billboard's U.S. Mainstream Rock Airplay chart, and "I Hate Everything About You" and "Animal I Have Become" had both passed one billion Spotify streams, making them the first Canadian band with two songs in the platform's Billions Club. That late-career resurgence reinforces their place as one of the most internationally durable Canadian hard-rock bands of the 2000s era.

Toronto emcee Thrust, born Christopher France, came up during the city's mid-1990s hip-hop expansion, when college radio, independent records and live showcases carried much of the scene's weight. His early work included the Past, Present, Future EP and the memorial track "Rage," while his stop-start flow and densely packed writing made him a distinctive voice among a generation building Canadian rap infrastructure before major-label attention became common. By the end of the decade, Exclaim! was already describing him as an artist who had spent years paying dues in the Toronto underground.

Thrust's widest national breakthrough arrived through the Rascalz' 1998 posse cut "Northern Touch," alongside Choclair, Kardinal Offishall and Vancouver's Checkmate. The record became a defining Canadian hip-hop statement, won the 1999 JUNO Award for Best Rap Recording and brought its featured artists onto the JUNO telecast one year after the Rascalz had protested the show's treatment of rap. Thrust used that visibility to lead into The Chosen Are Few, while his feature on soulDecision's "Faded" also placed a veteran Toronto rapper inside a Canadian pop hit that reached beyond the hip-hop audience.

Thrust matters as a connective figure rather than a one-record phenomenon. His career links Toronto's independent 1990s scene to "Northern Touch," a rare mainstream pop crossover and the long afterlife of Canadian rap history. He continued recording after his first wave of releases and later brought that experience into music education, giving his catalogue an additional role as living documentation of the years when Toronto hip-hop was developing its own networks, language and national visibility.

Saddle Lake Cree Nation singer-songwriter Tia Wood is a Plains Cree and Coast Salish Canadian artist whose soulful pop and R&B connects contemporary songwriting with the musical traditions of her community.

Toronto singer, songwriter and curator TiKA is a Canadian R&B and soul artist whose work combines rich vocals, Black queer storytelling and a long-running role in the city's independent music community.
St. John's singer-songwriter Tim Baker is a Canadian indie-folk and rock artist best known as the longtime frontman of Hey Rosetta! and for his later solo catalogue.

London, Ontario-born, Toronto-based rapper and producer Timbuktu is a veteran of Canadian underground hip-hop whose work spans solo releases, Backburner and groups including Swamp Thing and Teenburger.
Toronto turntablist, producer and touring DJ TLO is a Canadian hip-hop figure who won the Canadian DMC Supremacy title, represented Canada at the DMC World Finals and became Shad's longtime DJ.
Lagos-born, Brampton-raised singer and rapper TOBi is a Nigerian-Canadian artist whose music moves through hip-hop, R&B, jazz, soul and Afrobeat.

Born in Lynn Lake, Manitoba, and raised largely in Ontario, Tom Cochrane began as a folk-oriented singer-songwriter before joining Red Rider in the late 1970s. His writing helped give the band a distinctive place in Canadian rock: "White Hot" and "Lunatic Fringe" paired arena-ready musicianship with lyrics shaped by political unease and observation, while later Red Rider records produced songs including "Boy Inside the Man" and "Big League." By the end of the 1980s, Cochrane had already built a substantial career as one of the country's most recognizable rock songwriters.

His 1991 solo album Mad Mad World changed the scale of that career. The record reached Diamond status in Canada and sold millions worldwide, driven by "Life Is a Highway," a song whose combination of motion, resilience and enormous chorus became an international pop-rock standard. Cochrane continued recording solo while periodically returning to the Red Rider catalogue, and the durability of songs from both phases has kept his work present on Canadian radio and in live performance long after their original release cycles.

Cochrane's significance rests on more than one global hit. His catalogue links the socially alert rock of Red Rider to the expansive singer-songwriter sound of Mad Mad World, and his long-running humanitarian work has made public service part of the career rather than a separate activity. He was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 2003, and SOCAN honoured "Life Is a Highway" with its Cultural Impact Award in 2022, recognition of a song and songwriter deeply embedded in Canadian popular culture.
Toronto rapper Tona is a veteran Canadian MC known for densely written underground hip-hop, independent releases and collaborations with producers and lyricists across the country's rap scene.
Toronto production team Tone Mason makes hip-hop and R&B built around sample-based production, drum programming and songwriting, with credits spanning Canadian music, film and television.
Toronto rapper Top5, born Hassan Ali, is a Canadian hip-hop artist from Lawrence Heights whose drill-oriented music became a highly visible part of the city's 2010s rap scene.
Brampton-born rapper, singer and songwriter Tory Lanez is a Canadian R&B and hip-hop artist whose mixtapes and albums produced a long run of major Canadian and U.S. chart entries.

Touch is an Edmonton MC best known as part of the Canadian hip-hop duo Touch and Nato. His work is rooted in Alberta's long-running independent rap scene, with solo and collaborative recordings connecting him to Canadian underground hip-hop. Northern Dial carries Touch as part of its Edmonton hip-hop catalogue.

TRAPMAT SAVIOR is a Haiti-born, Montreal-based rapper whose work blends Quebec rap with melodic and experimental hip-hop influences. After moving to Montreal, he developed a distinctive style within the city's francophone scene and has been highlighted among emerging Quebec rap artists. Northern Dial carries TRAPMAT SAVIOR as part of its contemporary Montreal hip-hop catalogue.
Toronto rapper and producer Tre Mission is a Canadian grime pioneer whose music connects North American hip-hop with the U.K. grime scene through rapid-fire lyricism and bass-heavy production.

Treble Charger formed in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, when Greig Nori, Bill Priddle and Rosie Martin began recording the melodic indie-rock songs that became the independently released 1994 album NC17. After partnering with Hamilton label Sonic Unyon, the record became a major Canadian indie success and "Red" earned heavy college-radio and MuchMusic exposure. The band's early identity was rooted in the 1990s Canadian alternative underground, with power-pop melody and guitar noise arriving before the cleaner pop-punk sound that would later define its commercial peak.

After the major-label album Maybe It's Me, Treble Charger shifted dramatically on Wide Awake Bored. "American Psycho" became a Canadian hit and pushed the album to gold status, while "Brand New Low" reinforced the band's new, faster pop-punk direction. That transition placed Treble Charger directly between two eras of Canadian guitar music: the Sonic Unyon-centered indie network of the 1990s and the internationally successful pop-punk wave that followed. The band toured Summersault in 2000 alongside Our Lady Peace, Foo Fighters and the Smashing Pumpkins before releasing Detox in 2002.

Treble Charger's wider influence is inseparable from its connection to Sum 41. Nori managed and produced the Ajax band during its rise, and his work around that scene helped connect Treble Charger's stylistic pivot to the commercial explosion of Canadian pop-punk in the early 2000s. That relationship has become more complicated in later historical accounts, including serious allegations made by Deryck Whibley that Nori has denied. Musically, however, Treble Charger remains an important hinge in Canadian rock history: a band that began as an independent alternative act and helped make the vocabulary of pop-punk feel native to Canadian mainstream radio.
North Vancouver-born singer-songwriter Trevor Guthrie is a Canadian pop and dance vocalist known as the former frontman of soulDecision and for later electronic collaborations.

Trishannah is an Edmonton-based vocalist and multidisciplinary artist whose work spans solo performance, community arts and collaborative music projects. She has performed under the Trishannah Gentles Music name and has participated in Edmonton arts initiatives including 5 Artists One Love and CASA choir projects. Northern Dial carries Trishannah as part of its Alberta vocal and independent music catalogue.

Halifax hip-hop artist, producer and entrepreneur Tremayne 'Trobiz' Howe has been part of Nova Scotia's rap community since the early 1990s. A member of the early group The Overlords, he later became known for production work with artists including JRDN and Classified while also operating Fademasters in Halifax's North End.

Toronto duo TRP.P, formed by producer Truss and singer-songwriter pHoenix Pagliacci, is a Canadian R&B and hip-hop project known for queer love songs, soul-jazz influence and playful live performances.

Brampton-raised, Toronto-based Truss is a Canadian singer, rapper, songwriter, producer and audio engineer whose solo work and duo TRP.P blend hip-hop, R&B and soul. A self-taught multi-instrumentalist, he has composed for Canadian television, toured nationally and internationally and released solo projects including All Day Breakfast, Cavity, Root Canal and All We Ask Is Truss.

TwoTiime is an Ottawa rapper, singer and songwriter whose melodic street-rap combines hard-edged storytelling with emotionally direct hooks. He first drew national attention with Hood Cry and went on to build an Ottawa-rooted catalogue while expanding beyond the city's scene. Hood Cry, How I'm Comin and Up2Me are his three Northern Dial library credits.

TWOTWO is a Toronto rapper associated with More Real Entertainment and the city's street-rap scene. He broke through alongside Pengz on the 2017 Toronto hit Griselda Blanco before releasing solo tracks including Ball and Wrist and later reuniting with Pengz for Gangsta. Griselda Blanco is his Northern Dial library credit.
